## Worldview
Rome is a city of perhaps 700,000 to a million people and the capital of the Mediterranean, ruled in fact by one man: Caesar, dictator for ten years, back from the civil war in Africa. The Republic's forms survive, the Senate, the assemblies, the magistrates, and everyone wonders for how long. The gods are part of the state: augurs and haruspices read birds and entrails before public business, and prodigies are expiated. Educated Romans read Greek and choose among Stoics, Epicureans (who teach atoms and natural causes) and Academic sceptics, without experiment as a method. Medicine is Greek and practised mostly by Greek freedmen and slaves; disease comes from bad air, imbalance or the gods. Engineering is superb and empirical: aqueducts, sewers, roads, concrete, cranes. Labour is cheap because much of it is enslaved, so nobody looks for machines to save it. Numbers are Roman numerals, reckoned on the counting board; books are papyrus rolls copied by hand.

## People
- **Marcus Terentius Varro**: scholar, former Pompeian officer pardoned by Caesar, charged with organising Rome's first public library. Knows: Roman antiquities, Latin language, farming and stock breeding, the liberal arts including medicine; suspects that invisible animals from marshes cause disease. — Aged about 70, in Rome and on his estates (Reate, Casinum). Proscribed by Antony in 43 BC, loses his library but survives; writes De re rustica in 37 BC.
- **Themison of Laodicea**: Greek physician, the best-known pupil of Asclepiades, founder of the Methodic school. Knows: Asclepiades' medicine of particles and pores, treatment by diet, baths and regimen; said to be the first to use leeches. — Dates poorly known (c. 123–43 BC). Where he is in 46 BC is not recorded; he travelled widely (Crete, Milan) and may never have practised in Rome. Reachable only by search and letter.
- **Antistius**: physician in Caesar's circle. Knows: wound surgery. — Presumably in Rome in 46 BC. Known only from March 44 BC, when he examines Caesar's body and judges that of 23 wounds only the second, in the chest, was fatal.
- **Alexio**: Greek physician and friend of Cicero. Knows: Greek clinical medicine. — Practises in Rome in Cicero's circle. Dies suddenly in May 44 BC; Cicero mourns him as an excellent doctor.
- **Craterus**: fashionable Greek physician in Rome. Knows: Greek clinical medicine. — In Rome. Treats Attica, the young daughter of Atticus, in 45 BC (Cicero's letters to Atticus).
- **Asclapo of Patrae**: Greek physician in Achaea. Knows: Greek clinical medicine. — Nursed Cicero's secretary Tiro through an illness at Patrae; Cicero recommends him to the governor Servius Sulpicius Rufus about now. A voyage away.
- **Pompeius Lenaeus**: freedman of Pompey, grammarian and teacher in Rome. Knows: Greek and Latin; translated the pharmacological notes of Mithridates VI into Latin at Pompey's order. — In Rome in 46 BC, teaching after Pompey's death and loyal to his patron's memory.
- **Philodemus of Gadara**: Epicurean philosopher and poet, client of Calpurnius Piso (Caesar's father-in-law). Knows: Epicurean atomism, logic of inference from signs, a large Greek library. — Lives on the Bay of Naples; his library was probably the one found at Herculaneum. Dies around 40-35 BC.
- **Diodorus Siculus**: Greek historian from Agyrium in Sicily, working in Rome on his universal history. Knows: Egypt (visited about 60-56 BC), mines of Spain and Egypt, bitumen of the Dead Sea, alum of Lipari, geography from books. — In Rome through these years, an observer without office or patron of note.
- **Gaius Hirrius**: wealthy owner of sea-water fish ponds. Knows: breeding and keeping morays in salt-water ponds. — In or near Rome for the triumphs of 46 BC; where his ponds lie is not recorded. Lends Caesar morays for the triumphal banquets, by weight rather than for sale (2,000 in Varro, 6,000 in Pliny).
- **Sosigenes**: Astronomer who advised Caesar on the calendar. Knows: Greek and Egyptian calendar astronomy: the 365 1/4-day year, risings and settings of stars; Pliny also cites him on Mercury's greatest distance from the Sun. — Known almost only from Pliny the Elder; 'of Alexandria' is a later inference from the reform's Egyptian model. Presumably in Rome in 46 BC. Nothing is recorded of his later life.
- **Marcus Flavius**: Scribe (scriba) who assisted Caesar in drawing up the new calendar. Knows: The old pontifical calendar, the festival days and how the added days were placed so as not to move them. — Named only by Macrobius (Saturnalia 1.14). In Rome in 46 BC; nothing else is known of him.
- **Marcus Tullius Cicero**: Consular, orator, writer on philosophy. Knows: Translated Aratus' star poem into Latin; heard Posidonius on Rhodes; found Archimedes' tomb at Syracuse as quaestor in 75 BC; describes Archimedes' and Posidonius' planetary spheres; Stoic logic. — In Rome and at Tusculum in 46 BC, pardoned and politically idle; jokes that the stars now rise by edict. Writes his philosophical works in 45-44 BC. Killed in the proscriptions, 7 December 43 BC.
- **Vitruvius**: Military engineer serving under Caesar (artillery and siege machines). Knows: Cranes and tackles, catapult proportions, water clocks, sundials, pumps and water wheels as an engineer meets them; reads Greek mechanics. — Where he is in autumn 46 BC is not recorded, probably with the army. His ten books on architecture are twenty years in the future.
- **Publius Nigidius Figulus**: Senator, Pythagorean, astrologer and grammarian. Knows: Two books on the celestial sphere (Greek and non-Greek constellations), Egyptian astrology, divination, winds. — A Pompeian, in exile and reachable only by letter; where is not recorded. Cicero fails to win his pardon and he dies in exile in 45 BC.
- **Titus Pomponius Atticus**: Eques, financier, Cicero's friend and publisher. Knows: Lending at interest across Greece and Asia, bookkeeping, book production with trained slave copyists, Roman chronology (his Liber annalis). — In Rome in 46 BC, on good terms with every party. Survives the proscriptions of 43 BC; dies in 32 BC.
- **Lucius Cornelius Balbus**: Caesar's confidential agent in Rome, with Gaius Oppius; formerly his chief of engineers (praefectus fabrum). Knows: Caesar's finances and correspondence, including the ciphered letters; a native of Gades on the tidal Atlantic. — In Rome in 46 BC; with Oppius the way to Caesar's ear while Caesar is in Spain. Sides with Octavian after the murder; consul in 40 BC.
- **Gaius Oppius**: eques, Caesar's confidential agent in Rome with Balbus. Knows: Caesar's finances, correspondence (including the cipher) and intentions. — In Rome in 46 BC, running Caesar's affairs with Balbus while Caesar is in Spain. Later wrote on Caesar's life.
- **Marcus Tullius Tiro**: Cicero's freedman secretary (freed 53 BC). Knows: shorthand, dictation, editing and archiving letters and speeches. — With Cicero in Rome and at the villas. Outlives him and edits his papers.
- **Servius Sulpicius Rufus**: consul of 51 BC, the foremost jurist of the day. Knows: civil law treated as a system, the praetor's edict, legal opinions. — Governs Achaea for Caesar in 46 BC, reachable by letter or at Athens. Dies early in 43 BC on a Senate embassy to Antony at Mutina.
- **Aulus Ofilius**: jurist of equestrian rank, pupil of Servius, close to Caesar. Knows: civil law, the edict. — In Rome. The obvious man for Caesar's planned codification. Stays an eques and out of office.
- **Gaius Trebatius Testa**: jurist, protégé of Cicero, served on Caesar's staff in Gaul. Knows: civil law, Caesar's circle. — In Rome in 46 BC. Cicero dedicates the Topica to him in 44 BC. Lives on into Augustus' time.
- **Cratippus of Pergamon**: Peripatetic philosopher. Knows: Aristotelian philosophy, divination by dreams and frenzy (which he defends). — At Mytilene, then Athens. Cicero obtains Roman citizenship for him from Caesar; he teaches Cicero's son in 45–44 BC.
- **Gaius Cassius Longinus**: senator, pardoned Pompeian, saved the remnant of Crassus' army after Carrhae. Knows: Parthian tactics and the Syrian frontier at first hand, naval command, Epicurean philosophy. — In Italy in 46 BC (Rome, then Brundisium by January 45), pardoned; served Caesar against Pharnaces in 47 but kept out of the African war. Praetor in 44 BC and a leader of the murder; by 43 BC he holds Syria with an army.

## Events and timeline
- Every August to October (by the sun, not the drifting calendar): the fever season in Rome and the Campagna; those who can leave for the hills.
- 46 BC Feb: the regular intercalary month of 23 days is inserted (Caesar as pontifex maximus), bringing the year to 378 days.
- 46 BC Sep: Caesar's four triumphs (Gaul, Egypt, Pontus, Africa) on four days, with games and public feasts; awnings over the spectators are said to be silk, and Hirrius lends morays for the banquets. On 26 Sep, the last day, he dedicates the temple of Venus Genetrix and the unfinished Forum Iulium.
- 46 BC autumn: Caesar pardons M. Claudius Marcellus at the Senate's plea; Cicero breaks his silence with a speech of thanks (Pro Marcello).
- 46 BC: the free-grain list is recounted street by street through the landlords and cut from 320,000 to 150,000; juries limited to senators and equites; a sumptuary law (litters, purple, pearls, delicacies seized in the market); all but the ancient collegia dissolved; citizenship for physicians and teachers of the liberal arts in Rome.
- 46 BC, between November and December: two extra months totalling 67 days (intercalaris prior and posterior) are inserted; the year has 445 days.
- 46 BC late: Caesar leaves for Spain. Lepidus, consul and master of horse, runs Rome with six or eight prefects; Balbus and Oppius handle Caesar's business.
- 46–44 BC: in Syria the Pompeian Q. Caecilius Bassus holds Apamea against Caesar's generals and deals with the Parthians.
- 45 BC 1 Jan: the Julian calendar begins: 365 days, an extra day in February every fourth year, ten days spread over seven months. Told that Lyra rises tomorrow, Cicero answers: yes, by edict.
- 45 BC Jan–Feb: Cicero's daughter Tullia gives birth to a son and dies about a month later at Tusculum.
- 45 BC: Caesar's prefect Gaius Clovius issues coins of brass (orichalcum), a metal new to Roman coinage. Nigidius Figulus dies in exile.
- 45 BC: Cicero writes the Hortensius, Academica, De finibus and Tusculan Disputations, and begins On the Nature of the Gods, with Archimedes' tomb and the planetary spheres of Archimedes and Posidonius.
- 45 BC 17 Mar: battle of Munda. Caesar returns in the autumn and triumphs over Spain.
- 45–44 BC: Caesar plans to drain the Pomptine marshes, let out the Fucine Lake, build a harbour at Ostia and cut a canal through the Isthmus of Corinth.
- 45 BC 31 Dec: a consul dies on the last day of the year; Caesar has Caninius Rebilus elected consul for the remaining hours.
- 44 BC Jan–Feb: tribunes Flavus and Marullus deposed; Caesar named dictator for life; 15 Feb he refuses the diadem at the Lupercalia. Senate now about 900; colonies decreed at Carthage and Corinth; two aediles (ceriales) created for the grain supply. Quintilis is renamed Iulius among his honours.
- 44 BC 15 Mar: Caesar is killed at a Senate meeting in Pompey's theatre complex, three days before his planned departure for the Parthian war; the physician Antistius examines the body. The pontiffs, counting inclusively, will then add a leap day every third year until Augustus corrects it.

## Quest hooks
- A senator's household is sick with colic, pallor and weak wrists; the cellar master sweetens the wine with must boiled in lead pans
- Varro wants proof of his invisible marsh animals and has no instrument to see them
- Caesar will want the Pomptine marshes drained (44 BC); autumn fever empties every work camp there
- The newly enfranchised Greek physicians quarrel over a noble patient: bleed him or bathe him
- A glass merchant from Sidon shows a thin bubble of glass on the end of a tube and asks what it is good for
- Grain rots and heats in the Tiber warehouses while the dole list has just been halved
- A daughter of a great house lies in childbed fever days after the midwife left
- A perfumer from Capua would pay well for a way to capture the 'spirit' of wine or roses
- Veterans back from Africa have festering wounds and no physician who will touch them without a fee
- A swordsmith wants to know why Noric blades hold an edge and his own do not
- Get to Sosigenes or the scribe Flavius before the edict is final: the year is not 365 1/4 days but about 11 minutes shorter. Offer the rule of dropping three leap days in four centuries, and say how you know.
- The leap-year rule will be miscounted after Caesar's death, because Romans count inclusively. Have it written unambiguously into the edict or carved on a public calendar, against pontiffs who resent losing the calendar.
- Teach a banker's slave clerk place-value numerals with a sign for the empty column, on wax tablets, and race him against a master of the counting board in front of the Forum's money tables.
- Sail to Rhodes or Alexandria to find an instrument maker who can file bronze gear wheels, and bring back a geared planetary model, or a man able to build something new.
- Have a bronze founder and a turner build Ctesibius' twin-cylinder force pump from the Greek description and offer it for a city with no fire brigade and wooden tenements.
- Build a water-driven grain mill on a stream outside the city. The gearing is the hard part; a bakery owner with forty donkeys and slaves must be shown why he should care.
- A steam engine is wanted by nobody and lacks air pressure, a true cylinder and a sealed boiler. Show the weight of air with a pump and mercury first, and see who listens.
- Varro has a commission and no plan: what should Rome's first public library contain, how is it catalogued, who may read, and can anything be copied faster than a slave writes?
- The acta diurna are posted on a board and copied by whoever cares. Regular copies for the towns of Italy need a relay of riders that does not exist yet.
- Caesar wants the civil law reduced to order. Ofilius and Trebatius can draft; whoever shapes the plan decides what a citizen may claim against a magistrate.
- Debtors and creditors both curse the settlement of 49 BC, and the bankers at the Forum hoard coin. Anyone who can explain why coin disappeared has an audience among the equites.
- Caesar will march on Parthia in March 44 BC. Cassius knows what the arrows did at Carrhae; the army's cavalry rides without stirrups.
- Cicero is an augur who does not believe in augury and is about to say so in a book. A stranger who predicts something the augurs cannot will interest him and alarm the college.
- A banker at Puteoli lends on ships bound for Alexandria and hears of Greek pilots who cross from the Red Sea to India on one wind. Nobody in Rome has asked how.
- Caesar's cipher is a fixed shift of the alphabet; counting letters breaks it. Telling Balbus is either a great service or proof that the stranger reads Caesar's mail; Cicero would also love to know.
- Ostia has no harbour and Caesar wants one. Moles in the sea, a light, dredging: the engineers are at hand, the decision is his, and he leaves for Spain within weeks.
